items.summary: Triển vọng ngành bán dẫn tiếp tục được thúc đẩy bởi làn sóng AI và chuyển đổi số toàn cầu. Theo FedEx và Frost & Sullivan, thế giới dự kiến xy dựng hơn 2.000 trung tm dữ liệu mới trong giai đoạn 2026-2035. Sự phát triển của điện toán hiệu năng cao, mạng 5G và xe điện đang mở rộng nhu cầu đối với chip xử lý, chip nhớ cùng các giải pháp bán dẫn chuyên dụng. [...] Cùng với đó, hạ tầng nghiên cứu, nguồn điện ổn định và hệ thống logistics cần được phát triển đồng bộ. Đặc thù sản phẩm bán dẫn đòi hỏi độ chính xác cao, quy trình kiểm soát chất lượng nghiêm ngặt và thời gian giao hàng đáng tin cậy. Việc hoàn thiện các điều kiện nền tảng sẽ góp phần nng sức hấp dẫn đầu tư, đồng thời hỗ trợ doanh nghiệp trong nước tham gia su hơn vào chuỗi cung ứng. [...] Thành quả này cho thấy Việt Nam đã có những bước tiến cụ thể trong chuyển hóa năng lực nghiên cứu thành sản phẩm vi mạch. Dù chưa đồng nghĩa với việc làm chủ toàn bộ quy trình chế tạo bán dẫn, khả năng tự thiết kế chip chuyên dụng có ý nghĩa quan trọng, mở ra triển vọng phát triển các sản phẩm phục vụ an ninh, quốc phòng, công nghiệp và những lĩnh vực có nhu cầu bảo mật cao.

items.title: Doanh thu bán dẫn toàn cầu đạt kỷ lục 517,7 tỷ USD trong quý 3 - VnEconomy
items.summary:
Theo báo cáo mới đy của Hiệp hội Công nghiệp Bán dẫn Mỹ (SIA), doanh thu bán dẫn toàn cầu trong quý 3 ước đạt 517,7 tỷ USD, tăng gấp 2,5 lần so với cùng kỳ năm ngoái và tăng 24,1% so với quý trước.

Đy là lần đầu tiên doanh thu bán dẫn toàn cầu trong một quý vượt mốc 500 tỷ USD. Đáng chú ý, thị trường này đã ghi nhận mức tăng trưởng doanh thu khoảng 20% trong từng quý kể từ đầu năm. [...] Đà tăng trưởng này chủ yếu đến từ nhu cầu mua sắm đồng loạt các bộ tăng tốc AI và chip nhớ băng thông cao (HBM) của những doanh nghiệp vận hành các trung tm dữ liệu quy mô lớn.

Tính chung 9 tháng đầu năm, từ tháng 1 đến tháng 9, doanh thu bán dẫn toàn cầu đã vượt 1.219,5 tỷ USD, cao hơn 54% so với mức doanh thu kỷ lục 791,7 tỷ USD của cả năm ngoái.

Với tốc độ tăng trưởng hiện tại, doanh thu toàn ngành được dự báo sẽ vượt 1.600 tỷ USD vào cuối năm nay. [...] Trong các phn khúc bán dẫn, chip nhớ đang ghi nhận tốc độ tăng trưởng doanh thu nổi bật nhất.

Theo số liệu do Hiệp hội Công nghiệp Bán dẫn chu u phn tích, doanh thu chip nhớ toàn cầu trong quý 3 tăng 405,7% so với cùng kỳ năm ngoái. Trong khi đó, doanh thu chip logic, dòng chip đảm nhiệm các chức năng tính toán và điều khiển, chỉ tăng 61,9%.

Đà tăng trưởng vượt trội của chip nhớ chủ yếu xuất phát từ nhu cầu DRAM gia tăng, trong khi giá bán các sản phẩm cũng liên tục leo thang.

items.title: RAG vs. Graph RAG vs. Agentic RAG, clearly explained!
items.summary:
RAG vs. Graph RAG vs. Agentic RAG, clearly explained!

Standard RAG embeds documents into vectors and retrieves the most similar chunks via similarity search. For direct factual lookups, this works well.

But it breaks down when a query needs to connect facts spread across multiple documents. Similarity search retrieves individual chunks, not the relationships between them.

Graph RAG adds a knowledge graph layer on top.

→ During indexing, an LLM extracts entities and relationships from the documents.

→ During retrieval, the system traverses these connections instead of relying on embedding similarity alone.

This is what enables multi-hop queries.

Say a vector DB stores three facts about internal services:

↳ "The checkout service uses payments API."
↳ "The payments API runs on cluster-3."
↳ "Cluster-3 is scheduled for maintenance on Friday."

Someone asks: "Will the checkout service be affected by Friday's maintenance?"

Vector search can likely retrieve facts 1 and 3 because the query mentions "checkout service" and "Friday maintenance."

But it will miss fact 2, which connects the payments API to cluster-3.

That middle fact sits too far from the query in embedding space. It mentions neither "checkout" nor "maintenance," so it never makes it into the retrieved context.

A knowledge graph connects these as linked entities, and graph traversal finds the full path in one query.

Agentic RAG takes a different approach entirely.

Instead of a fixed retrieval pipeline, an LLM agent decides at query time which tools to invoke, which sources to query, and in what order.

Check the visual below to understand the three architectures thoroughly.

One thing to note here is that these three aren't levels of sophistication that you need to graduate through.

Instead, they solve different query types.

↳ Single-hop factual lookups → standard RAG
↳ Multi-hop relationship queries → Graph RAG
↳ Dynamic multi-source tasks with tool use → Agentic RAG

Once the right architecture is in place, the next leverage point is efficiency.

Most RAG architectures rely heavily on vector search, and that layer can be made 32x more memory-efficient using binary quantization.

I covered the full implementation in the article below.

👉 Over to you: Which RAG architecture are you running in production?

items.title: RAG vs. Vectorless RAG, clearly explained!
items.summary:
RAG vs. Vectorless RAG, clearly explained!

In a standard RAG setup, documents are split into chunks, embedded, and stored in a vector DB. The query gets embedded too, and the top-k closest chunks go to the LLM.

The problem is that similarity and relevance answer different questions.

For instance, five annual reports from one company can likely follow the same template every year, and only the numbers can change.

So a FY2022 question can lie just as close to an FY2025 chunk, and the LLM might answer from the wrong year.

Cross-references introduce another problem. If a chunk mentions "see Appendix G" but looks nothing like the table in Appendix G, that table will never make it to the top-k.

Vectorless RAG drops the embedding model and the vector DB, and replaces similarity search with LLM reasoning instead.

The preprocessing step parses each document's layout into a ToC tree index. Every node holds a section title, its page range, and a short summary, and the whole tree fits in the LLM's context.

At query time, the LLM gets the query along with the tree. It reads the section titles and summaries and picks the few sections most likely to hold the answer.

For example, for a question about debt, it might pick the "Financial Summary" section and also "Appendix G", because its summary says the debt details are there.

The system then pulls those full sections and checks whether the evidence is enough.

↳ If it is, the LLM answers from the full sections, with page citations.
↳ If not, it goes back to the tree and opens more nodes.

The LLM also sees the chat history. So if you ask about assets and then follow up with "what about liabilities?", it goes back to the same report.

The trade-off is that every query now runs LLM calls over the tree.

Top-k vector search will be cheaper in that same run (although not guaranteed to be as accurate), and the tree only helps when documents have real structure.

So the two suit different data:

↳ Use a tree for long, structured documents like filings, contracts, and manuals.
↳ Stick with a vector DB for lots of short, unrelated text.

The diagram below depicts both flows.

If you want to dive deeper, I have also written a full breakdown of MIT's Recursive Language Models.

It covers why LLMs get worse as context grows and how RLMs let the model split a long document and work through it piece by piece.

Read it below.

items.title: BYE-BYE TO TRADITIONAL WEB SCRAPING!!
items.summary:
BYE-BYE TO TRADITIONAL WEB SCRAPING!!

Someone just built PixelRAG.

Instead of turning websites into plain text, it takes screenshots and uses a vision-language model to read information directly from the pixels.

That’s a big deal.

Traditional scraping often loses important information like:

→ PDFs
→ Tables
→ Layouts
→ Buttons
→ Columns

All of that can disappear when a webpage is converted into plain text.

PixelRAG takes a different approach:

It indexes pages exactly as they appear to the human eye.

The team has already built a visual index of Wikipedia with over 30 million screenshots.

And it reportedly beats the best text-based RAG by 18.1% on QA.

It also comes with a plugin for Claude Code.

Basically, it gives Claude eyes.

Pass it a URL, an arXiv paper, or a local website, and Claude doesn’t need to scrape the DOM.

It can actually look at the page.

Here’s how it works:

→ Builds a FAISS index
→ Searches visually across pixels
→ Embeds content with Qwen3-VL-Embedding
→ Converts websites, PDFs, and images into tiles

Fully open source under Apache-2.0.

Link to the repo in the comments 👇🏻

items.summary:
𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗼 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱 𝗮 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻-𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗱𝘆 𝗔𝗜 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗶𝗻 𝟳 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀

A demo proves an AI agent can work.

Production proves it can work reliably, securely, and at scale.

Here are the 7 essential engineering stages.

𝟭. 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿 | 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺 & 𝗦𝘂𝗰𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀
Define the use case, target users, measurable KPIs, and risks (security, privacy, bias).
𝟮. 𝗗𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻 | 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗔𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲
Choose ReAct or Plan-Execute, define decision flows, guardrails, and human approval points.
𝟯. 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗰𝘁 | 𝗧𝗼𝗼𝗹𝘀 & 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆
Integrate APIs, manage context and memory, and enforce least-privilege tool access.

𝟰. 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁 | 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗜𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀
Build structured prompts, function schemas, few-shot examples, and output constraints.
𝟱. 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱 | 𝗥𝗔𝗚 & 𝗞𝗻𝗼𝘄𝗹𝗲𝗱𝗴𝗲
Prepare and chunk data, implement keyword/vector retrieval, and enforce source permissions.
𝟲. 𝗧𝗲𝘀𝘁 | 𝗘𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 & 𝗥𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆
Test accuracy, hallucinations, prompt injection, tool failures, latency, and cost.

𝟳. 𝗗𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆 | 𝗟𝗟𝗠𝗢𝗽𝘀 & 𝗢𝗯𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆
Use CI/CD, tracing, monitoring, alerts, versioning, and rollback mechanisms.
𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗠𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗧𝗲𝗮𝗺𝘀 𝗠𝗶𝘀𝘀
• No clear KPIs → No way to measure value.
• Poor grounding → Unreliable responses.
• Weak guardrails → Unauthorized actions.
• Missing evaluations → Failures reach users.
• No observability → Difficult incident recovery.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆
𝗟𝗟𝗠 + 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁 + 𝗧𝗼𝗼𝗹𝘀 = 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗼𝘁𝘆𝗽𝗲
𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 + 𝗚𝘂𝗮𝗿𝗱𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘀 + 𝗘𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘀 + 𝗢𝗯𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 = 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀

Building an agent is easy. Engineering one you can trust is the real challenge.

items.title: A new technique just made attention 23x faster!
items.summary:
A new technique just made attention 23x faster!

At 10M tokens, sparse attention slows down not because of attention itself but rather because of deciding which keys to attend to.

Let's understand why and how a new technique solves it without scanning every key.

1) Full attention at long context:

In full attention, every query is compared against every earlier key. This leads to O(T^2) complexity for prefill, and at 10M tokens it dominates the forward pass.

2) Sparse attention:

Sparse attention lets each query read only a small set of <k> keys instead of all of them, so the attention becomes cheap.

But something still has to pick those <k> keys, and at long context, this step becomes the bottleneck.

3) Why picking keys is still quadratic:

DeepSeek's DSA uses a lightning indexer that scores every earlier key. GLM-5.3-Flash pools 4 keys into 1 before scoring. NSA, MoBA, and Quest score blocks of nearby keys.

Each of them scans the whole context for every query, so the indexer stays O(T^2), and at 10M tokens, it takes 98% of the layer's time.

Block methods have another issue. Blocks group keys by position, so one relevant key within filler can get averaged away in the block summary.

4) How LSA picks keys:

Latent Sparse Attention (LSA) is a new approach that groups keys by meaning instead of position.

- Each key is projected into a 64-dim index space, and every 4 consecutive keys are pooled into one.

- When a 512-key block fills up, it's clustered into buckets of ~8 similar keys, with one centroid per bucket. Finished blocks are never rebuilt.

- A query scores only the centroids, keeps the top 1,024 buckets, and expands them into 4,096 keys, plus 4 sink tokens and the 512 most recent keys.

- Exact FlashAttention then runs over that list with an unchanged kernel.

If you've built RAG, this is like cluster-based vector search running inside attention. The kernel design even cites FAISS.

At 10M tokens, LSA's prefill is 72.4x faster than full attention on Qwen-3.8-27B and 22.7x faster than GLM-5.3-Flash's own sparse attention.

The time to first token improves:

- 9.2x on Qwen
- 2.2x on GLM

Below ~512k tokens, it's roughly break-even.

Here's the paper: https://t.co/ZLs6hONXg1

That said, LSA attempts to find the keys more cheaply, not storing them. The KV cache still grows linearly with context, and at 10M tokens, managing that memory becomes the next engineering problem.

I wrote an article on how 12 ways serving systems handle it, covering paging, offloading, quantizing, and more.

Read it below.
